headline: Japan Celebrates 107,677 Centenarians—A Milestone of Long Life
meta_description: Japan has crossed a historic threshold with over 100,000 people aged 100 or older, the highest number in the world. Most are women.
summary_short: Japan now has 107,677 centenarians—more than any other nation. The milestone reflects decades of progress in medicine and healthy living habits.
body:
For the first time, Japan is home to more than 100,000 people aged 100 or older. The health ministry reports 107,677 centenarians in the island nation—the highest number globally—with women comprising 88 percent of this remarkable population. Kishimoto Fuyo, a 114-year-old from Kyoto City, is the country's oldest person, while the oldest man, Kato Hikaru, is 112. Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno expressed delight at seeing so many people living long, healthy, and active lives, pointing to advances in medicine and technology as key drivers of this achievement.

Experts attribute Japanese longevity to lifestyle and diet. The traditional cuisine emphasizes fish, vegetables, and rice while limiting saturated fats—a stark contrast to many Western diets. Older adults remain physically active, regularly walking, cycling, and using public transport. Companies have responded to this aging population with innovations including powered exoskeletons to aid mobility and eyewear that automatically adjusts focus. The milestone will be celebrated during Japan's annual "Respect for the Aged" public holiday, when the government honors those turning 100 with a personal letter and traditional sake cup.

Yet this celebration masks a profound demographic challenge. Japan's total fertility rate fell to a record low of 1.14 last year, well below the 2.1 needed for population replacement. The country's total population is projected to decline 30 percent by 2070, dropping from its 2008 peak of 128 million to just 87 million. Already, those aged 65 and older make up nearly 30 percent of the population and are expected to represent almost 40 percent within decades. Government subsidies encouraging young people to have children have failed to reverse the trend. Immigration remains limited, with foreigners comprising only about 3 percent of the population.
quick_facts: 107,677 centenarians in Japan—the world's highest number
Kishimoto Fuyo, 114, is Japan's oldest person
Japan's fertility rate dropped to record low of 1.14
